b: When it came to the candidates who will hold office and represent the people, the midterms were an overwhelming success for the freedom to read.
When it came to state- and local-level policies, referendums, and amendments, the midterms were much less successful.

With the results settling and the reality of 2027 just a little over a month away, literary advocates can continue their efforts to support anti-book ban, pro-public library, pro-public education. There’s a lot on the table across the country, and each step an individual takes builds the kind of momentum that helped ignite change, as we saw at the ballot box this month.
Support Florida. Don’t Denigrate It or Write It Off.

Florida did not “go blue” the way that Texas did, but races across the state were tremendously close. Several major democratic wins occurred in the very areas that republicans deliberately gerrymandered. Those republicans spent a lot of money on their candidates and their ballot measures, and the fact that several democrats came within just a few points of winning both showcases that Florida isn’t a “lost cause”. It highlights how deeply impacted voters are in the state by voter suppression, gerrymandering, and disenfranchisement. Rather than write off the state, it’s beyond high time for advocates to pay attention to and support those doing tremendous work on the ground to protect access to books, libraries, and public education.

One of the biggest disappointments from the midterms in Florida was the passage of Amendment 3. More than 60% of voters supported tax cuts, which state Republicans sold as a way to ease their financial challenges. What those republicans did not say–and that libraries, firefighters, and other municipal services both within and beyond the state shouted about for over a year before voters saw their ballot–was that this meant local service funding would be decimated. Homeowners may pay less on their properties, but that could mean potentially devastating bills if they need to use services like fire or ambulance services or their public libraries.

Public libraries in Florida are already bracing for impact. Many ran the numbers before the election, noting that they might need to slash their budgets by 60 or 70 percent. That means significant cuts to staff and materials, which trickle down to cuts in hours and online services. With the uncertain future of the Federal Communications Commission’s E-Rate–an affordable way for libraries and schools to provide internet services at their facilities–this could be the kind of mass disenfranchisement not seen in generations.

Understand that libraries across the state have been begging for help for years. They’ve had to do so quietly, for fear of retaliation from the state. This includes the state’s library association. Their lack of posting calls to action isn’t by choice; it’s by force, and it’s abetted by tremendous fear of being targeted by politicians.
Here’s what library advocates can do in the face of what feels like an insurmountable hurdle for libraries in Florida.

When service changes happen at public libraries, explicitly name why this is. It was Amendment 3, voted for by over 60% of state residents, in the 2026 Midterm elections. Yes, it was widely reported on. Yes, this means you lost your library and its robust services because your tax money pays for those things.
Then, be a library hyper person. Shared by Marion County Library System, this graphic has some very easy ways to advocate for the library every single day.

Get involved in your library’s Friends of the Library group or its Foundation. Either/both–they’re different organizations, to be clear–fundraise on behalf of the library. They are independent of the library, and in many cases, they have far greater ability to advocate on behalf of libraries than the libraries themselves. If you’re involved, encourage this kind of advocacy and help spearhead initiatives to raise funds for the library. If your library does NOT have a Friends group, consider starting one. Learn from the library how this might operate, whether there’s been one in the past, and where to get started. United for Libraries offers numerous resources to help launch or revive Friends of the Library groups.

Follow your local library and take direction from them. Every library operates differently, and each will be surmounting unique hurdles. In some libraries, it will be staffing; in others, hours; in still others, collections. Because of the state of fear that may further silence libraries, go into your local library and ask to talk with them about what you and others like you can do to help them. Here’s a great example from Miami-Dade–as shared by their Friends of the Library–and a great example of communication from Broward County Library’s Foundation. Another great example, as shared by their Friends of the Library group, comes from Ocala. As noted in the previous bullet, Friends and Foundations are going to be crucial communicators on behalf of libraries in addition to their role as fundraisers.

Understand that what you’re allowed to borrow from your library may change. Whatever that looks like, know that utilizing the library is especially crucial right now and into the future. Borrow all the books you can, attend every program that you can, try out the digital resources from home, and encourage everyone to do the same. Now is the time to get your library card if you don’t have one. Coordinate a library date with friends or family members who also need to get one.

Call your state-level representatives in support of local libraries and encourage them to fight to protect library services as core services, the way public schools are in the new law. Tell them what is at stake and why they need to push for exceptions and carveouts to Amendment 3. The legislature must pass laws to implement the amendment, so your voice is especially important right now. DeSantis only has so long to do the job before his term expires, and the work would fall to the incoming (republican) governor. Your voice can impact where and how the library piece of this comes into play.

Follow and engage with advocacy happening both in and beyond the state. EveryLibrary has set up a website and campaign to keep Florida libraries open, and groups like the Florida Freedom to Read Project have been on the ground covering censorship issues in libraries for years.
Of note: a similar tax slashing scheme in Wyoming did not pass, which is good news for municipalities in that state.

There hasn’t been much news to report on the slate of book banning bills and the defunding of the Institute of Museum and Library Services since mid-August. That’s because republican leadership decided to put the House on an extended recess until after the midterms to avoid impeachment talk for Pete Hegseth. The House is back in session, as is the Senate, and though it is a lame duck session, republicans will use whatever they can to pass their bad bills with significant consequences to the American people.
That means even now, continue to reach out to your current federal representatives and future ones about the following issues.

Funding the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS): Earlier this year, Trump zeroed out the Fiscal Year 2027 budget to the only federal agency overseeing public libraries for the sixth time. Right now, the federal government is operating under a Continuing Resolution, which will expire on December 11. That means if they don’t pass a budget before then, the federal government will once again shut down until one passes. The IMLS needs your advocacy to ensure that its minuscule budget gets passed for the coming fiscal year. IMLS was already gutted in the first months of this administration; it needs every penny it can get, and we the people deserve to see our public libraries and museums have access to federal capital.

House Resolution 7661 (HR 7661): One of the first bills to mandate book bans nationwide, HR 7661’s status today is the same that it was in mid-August. It’s on the Union Calendar, meaning that it is eligible to be heard by the full House at any time. Here’s what to know about this specific bill and what actions to take–in addition to what’s here, this is a potent opportunity to reach out to new House representation you may have for next year and get in their ears about it now.

Senate Bill 4925 (S 4925): This is the Senate’s companion bill to HR 7661. The status of this bill is the same as it was in mid-August, with the bill being referred to the Senate’s Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) committee. This is what the bill would do, and in terms of action, reach out to your Senators about it, especially if they’re on the HELP committee. If you have a new Senator or two coming in next year, get in touch with them now.

House Resolution 2616 (HR 2616): This is a national “Don’t say trans” bill that would ban any education–including access to books–related to “gender ideology” in public schools. This bill already passed the House and it is currently in the Senate. It’s in the Senate HELP committee, so like with S 4925, get in touch with your current and future Senators, especially if you have one on the HELP committee.

House Resolution 8705 (HR 8705): The “CHARLIE” Act would withhold funding from public schools that teach racial and gender inclusivity, creating the opportunity for rampant book bans. This one passed out of a House committee, but it has not made its way to the union calendar for full House consideration. This is where you get in touch with current and forthcoming House representation in opposition to the bill.

Another thing you can do now is reach out to the teams working for your 2027 representatives, whether or not they’re the same people who have been representing you. Ask for a 15-minute phone call to talk about issues important to you–whether that’s directly with the congressional representatives or with their team. Then, talk about where and how library advocacy matters to you and where and how you’ll be supporting efforts for them to vote pro-library, pro-literacy, and pro-public education during their tenure.

If you don’t have that time or can’t get it, send it via email and/or leave a short message. Make sure your representatives are saved in your contacts and reach out to them regularly to address legislative concerns. Be annoying in your consistency. Those who are fighting hard to yank our rights from us are, and don’t care that they are.

Once you’ve done that, share it with your networks and encourage them to do it, too. Be the light others need to see. Want to take a bonus step? Write a script for each of the above bills that you can share with friends and family to use when they reach out to their representatives.
In States That Turned Blue (and Those That Did Not)

States that saw their representation shift from republican–whether temporary or deeply entrenched–to democratic have a tremendous opportunity to take advantage of what’s happened. This is where you begin contacting your new representation, introducing yourself, highlighting your priorities, and holding those leaders accountable.

Prepare yourself by getting their phone numbers and email addresses in your contacts. Find out where their local offices are, and keep tabs on when they’re working in the community. Show up to those town halls and meetings and come prepared with questions about their work related to issues on libraries and education. You may not yet have access to their DC information if they’re representing you at the federal level; make it a task to find that out in the new year.

This is also where advocacy on bad bills already enrolled in your state becomes important, too. Many of the bad library and bad literary bills which have passed may be hard to overturn; instead, look to where and how you can get involved in starting the process of changing those laws and/or building new legislation that nullifies what is on the books. A huge messaging opportunity exists here, particularly as many of the most ardent book banning legislators have lost their elections–people voted legislators like Ken Ivory out in Utah because he was so obsessed with banning books in schools, rather than actual issues facing Utahns (repeat for any number of other candidates).

It is true that Freedom to Read laws are meaningful, and that they’re also faulty. Books still get banned even in states with laws like these because most of these laws are without mechanisms to change local-level decisions. Maryland is an example of where and how these teeth matter, and its law is one to look to as a model for what is possible elsewhere. While it sounds silly to some to think a state like Kansas may be able to pass an anti-book ban law, don’t laugh–Kansas was among the states that have tried to pass such legislation, and that was before it had more democratic representation.

Another worthwhile action to take in newly blue states: building and strengthening freedom-to-read coalitions. Many of these states already have on-the-ground groups doing the work, but they could use even more support and engagement now. Find out if there’s a group near you, and if not, consider where and how you can launch one (here’s a guide from 2022 on how to start a local anti-censorship group that’s still relevant!). If you’re a library worker and not already involved in your state library association, that’s another great place to begin–and whether you’ll be a new member or are a long-time member of a state library association, get involved in that organization’s intellectual freedom committee. No such committee exists? Get one going. The more library professionals actively engaged in freedom to read committee work–which can include providing support for challenges occurring in the state, developing resources for library workers, offering education or events related to intellectual freedom, among other things–the more community and coalition building there is. Library workers and grassroots organizations have a prime opportunity to work together here, too. The work is mutually beneficial, not exclusive nor hierarchical.

If you live in a solidly blue state, this is also your opportunity to reach out to your newly-blue colleagues and those who are still in solidly-red states. We do better when we all work together, no matter where we live and the luck we have in our representation in those places.

Something else to do, especially in newly blue and still red states: document, document, document. In a forthcoming Literary Activism piece, I’ll be talking about where and how the actions and history related to book bans in the 2020s are disappearing right before our eyes–a prime opportunity for those who’ve been leading the charge to lie about their involvement and what actually happened. We must continue to document and archive what’s happening, why it happened, and who exactly was involved. Continue to pay attention to the bad actors both in the legislature and on the ground; name them, collect evidence, and commit to publicly noting and sharing this so it does not get erased or forgotten.
Ongoing Action at the Local and State Level

Everything above is applicable, no matter where you live. But if anything is to be learned from five years of on-the-ground anti-censorship work it’s this: local level work is what creates ripple effects upstream.

Despite the realities that Americans are facing election fatigue and burnout, many will be back at the polls in the spring to vote for school and library board members. Given what happened in the midterms, do not be surprised to see a rush of far-right interest in these positions. What was lost in “higher” positions may be seen as an opportunity to once again flood the local level with their politics, even and especially in so-called “nonpartisan” seats.

This is the time to consider developing voter guides for these elections. Frank Strong shared how to build a voter guide for school board elections last year, and I put together one for how to build a voter guide for public library elections. If you have capacity and passion, consider where or how you might run for office yourself–filing deadlines will be coming up soon.

Begin to look at where and how legislators are pre-filing bills that would affect public schools, public libraries, and access to books. You can do this by searching Legiscan, limiting the search to your state (or any state of interest), and using keywords like “library” or “education.” Make sure you are looking at bills for 2027, though looking at historic bills can help identify legislators who may not be friendly to protecting the right to read. Of note: if there’s been a prefiled bill by a legislator who did not get reelected to their seat, those bills will be null and void unless someone else chooses to sponsor them.

It should be emphasized that the work is far from done. Even if we ever reach a world where all the anti-library, anti-education, and anti-book bills disappear, we still live in a world where the people whose stories and voices are being erased by such legislation are seeing their rights stolen in other ways. In “good” “blue” states, trans folks saw voters put their best interests out of mind. Washington residents voted for gender testing for high school athletes, putting girls through the humiliating and cruel experience of having someone confirm their gender before they can play sports. Washington residents who find this sickening can still do something here–write your school districts and demand they refuse to follow the law (this is already happening, and the same people who demanded school districts choose not to enforce COVID vaccines are now mad that other people are demanding districts not discriminate against trans youth).
All of these fights are connected, and it’s our duty to speak up and out where and how we can.

There are many ways to get and stay engaged after the midterms. But don’t stop here. Another excellent recent resource is this four-step, post-election advocacy challenge from the Freedom to Read Project. I think the last point is especially vital, as we have a real opportunity to engage friends and family on these issues in a way that we have not successfully done so far. Wins like the ones we saw this month matter, and they make advocacy feel more realistic and achievable to those who’ve sat it out.

Celebrating victories matters. Do that, and roll up your sleeves on the next actions to take. The year isn’t over, and we’ve got the opportunity and the obligation to make next year one where our politicians know they answer to us.

Ken Ivory, one of the biggest champions of Utah’s book banning law, was voted out of office. That’s going to make the work being done by Utah Parents United/LaVerna in the Library/RatedBooks/The National Book Rating Index a little bit harder since he was a real advocate of it.

There are new rules being proposed by the Sarah Huckabee-appointed Arkansas State Library Board to further restrict access to books in public libraries. This is thanks in no small part to the approval of Act 372 by the courts this summer.
An anonymous Arkansas librarian talks about what’s at stake for libraries and library workers in the state.

Here’s another article about how AI is being used to ban books. We’ve had a number of them lately, but it’s not a new tactic. It was first used in a very public way in 2023. I wish more of these let the actual experts on the ground offer more context, insight, and action items.

The Readington School Board (NJ), which decided to ban The Perks of Being a Wallflower–despite the state’s anti-book banning law–and they’re arguing about how to word what they did in their press release. Almost as if wording and interpretation of wording is in the eyes of the reader.
Here’s how eighth graders in Readington schools responded to the removal of Stephen Chbosky’s book.
In some good news, Wisconsin Books to Prisoners is able to send books to those on the inside again.

Did you know when book banners read the book they want to ban and don’t simply rely on the cherry-picked passages someone handed them, they can change their minds? Here’s how, with the example of All Boys Aren’t Blue by George M. Johnson.

“Layne Craig made an uncommon appeal to Fort Worth ISD’s [TX] state-appointed board of managers: Dismantle the school library advisory council she leads. An educator and mom of two FWISD students, Craig said the council, often shortened to SLAC, was generating needless hurdles for librarians attempting to buy books for their campuses. “I believe that SLAC is a hindrance to our district’s librarians that does not provide a meaningful service to Fort Worth ISD parents and students,” Craig told managers Nov. 10. The state-appointed managers on Tuesday voted 7-0 to dissolve the school library advisory council.” It’s what literally everyone has said since the start, and it’s great she used her time to make the statement–and that she was heard is huge. I think we’re going to see more of this happen across Texas because I do think that the state’s obsession with books in libraries will be slowing with their new leadership.
A new report out of Florida explores where and how school board members have been impacted by state pressure.

The Florida Attorney general is investigating claims from parents who enrolled their students in a private school that the school violated their parental rights because they utilized books that the parents didn’t like. This’ll be curious to watch.

This story is paywalled, but the pull quote is excellent. There’s a new potential plan in Northern Ireland that would open the door to book bans in libraries. Pull quote: “‘We’ve seen what’s happened in America and we can’t let it happen here’, says author.”
